newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION-Louthean on Australian Mining - Platinum proves elusive.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Louthean on Australian Mining - Platinum proves elusive.

text.p: *By Ross Louthean
As one door closes, another opens for Australia's elusive quest for a platinum mine. Nevertheless it is still a rocky road.

The high hopes for an Alaska-style deposit at Fifield in New South Wales and for Bushveld-style finds in the ultramafic complexes at Weld Range, Munni Munni and the Windimurra prospects have been dented but not totally dispelled. Indeed, Weld Range, now a joint venture between Dragon Resources NL and Sons of Gwalia Ltd is showing a new hope for Australia s great white metal hope -- the discovery of nickel which broadens the scope from platinum group metals (PGM) to something more polymetallic.
The tempo for nickel exploration in Australia has grown and with it has the scope for PGM by association or being found in greater consequences through more diverse and possibly deeper exploration.
The seekers include some newcomers. Tulloch Resources NL, now seeking listing, has a group of nickel-PGM targets in Western Australia including the Plumridge target in the north eastern goldfields.

Then there is Defiance Mining NL which mothballed plans to re-establish nickel-copper mining at Carr Boyd, north east of Kalgoorlie, to go back into broader brush exploration in a mafic-ultramafic complex enveloping the area.

The catch-cry here, and in many other Australian prospecting locales, is a suite with a geological analogy to Voisey's Bay, the great Canadian nickel find with great cobalt, copper and precious metals values.

Defiance picked up significant platinum values seven years ago at the quaintly named "Piss of Hill". This had been the movie set in the early 1980s for a drilling scene in the Googie Withers film "The Nickel Queen" where drillers had used rocks to write a message to tell stockbrokers and speculators flying over the area to go away. (The scene was based on fact, except the real drillers used more pithy language to tell the airborne
nosey-parkers to go away).
Defiance's focus then was on enhancing nickel resources around Carr Boyd. Now it is into more regional work using a geological model.

One of the great platinum hopes of the late 1980s was Munni Munni when a large but sub-economic PGM-gold resource was outlined in a Bushveld-style system. Now, Hunter is a subsidiary of gold producer Eagle Mining Corp NL which in 1996 lifted the mothballs off this project to try and delineate wider and higher grade zones.
This work also saw Eagle open up a case for not only a Voisey's Bay model but to also look at depth away from the PGM reef for a large copper-gold play similar to one found in Greenland.

The main nickel play still appears to be Weld Range, where late in 1996 Dragon Mining-Sons of Gwalia (SGW) found a large lateritic nickel-cobalt system. Weld Range has not been intensely drilled to prove or disprove its validity, for Dragon and previous partner Burmine Ltd (now merged with SGW) had other pre-occupations.
But the picture has become more polymetallic and Dragon said it has also come up with another chromiferous horizon that extends into its Range Well ferrochrome joint venture.

The leading light of the 1980s was the Fifield region where Helix Resources NL covered several intrusions including Owendale and Tout While Helix came up with PGM in several sequences and the Hillview vermiculite deposit at Girilambone to the north, they did not advance to an economic criteria.

Helix became flavour of the year in 1996 with its spectacular Lake Everard gold discovery in South Australia's Gawler Craton and it moved messing and accommodation facilities from Fifield to the Gawler Craton.
This immediately downgrades Fifield, but cashed up Helix may produce a gold mine which will allow it to return to Fifield for a more deeper probe.

The other Fifield property that remains alive in Syerston held by Australian Uranium NL NOR.AX (formerly Noble Resources NL.) This is a massive low grade polymetallic target with significant values of nickel, cobalt, PGM and chromite.

While the big picture for Australian Uranium is its uranium holdings in the Northern Territory the company will also continue a focus on Syerston which in 1997 will include more drilling and studies on ore characteristics and possible mineral processing techniques.

One of the other revived PGM projects is Mulga Springs which was placed in the portfolio of 1996 float Golden Cross Resources NL. Mulga Springs had produced some spectacular PGM and nickel-copper grades when explored in the 1980s by Mumbill Mines NL, a then listed subsidiary of Delta Gold NL.
Mumbill-Delta had not been able to piece the knitting together and eventually dropped the area.

Late in 1996 Golden Cross produced more spectacular results at Moorkei and Little Darling Creek, along strike from Mulga Springs. Systematic rock chip sampling on an ultramafic intrusive included a best line of 20.6 grams/tonne platinum, 38 g/t palladium, 0.59 g/t gold, 2.95 percent cooper, 0.07 percent cobalt and 1.88 percent nickel.
A bold new face has appeared with the listing of Australian Platinum Mines NL (APM), a company cobbled together by Sydney stockbroker Alan Doyle.
APM has the Copper Hills prospect in the Pilbara hinterland of WA, south of the Rudall River National Park and RTZ-CRA Ltd's Kintyre uranium-rich polymetallic project.

The company has earmarked several targets for more detailed exploration, following up on exploration undertaken several years ago by several explorers including CRA Exploration, Power & Nuclear Corp of Japan and North Flinders Mines Ltd.

The quest for Australia to produce a platinum mine remains hamstrung by political correctness. The first real chance was to come from the Coronation Hill gold-PGM project in the NT which was arbitrarily spiked by then Prime Minister Robert Hawke.

Meanwhile, one of the great untouched PGM targets - the Giles Complex which straddles WA and SA remains hamstrung by Aboriginal land rights politics where nothing proceeds and everybody loses, except of course the lawyers.
*Ross Louthean is editor of Paydirt and GoldMining Journal and publisher of the new Australian Mines Handbook
